title: Can, want, must: the verb bracket (können, wollen, müssen)
summary: Say what you can, want and have to do. The second verb goes to the end: Ich kann heute nicht kommen.
goals: Use können, wollen and müssen with every person
Put the second verb at the end (the verb bracket)
Say what you don't have to do: Ich muss nicht ...

nicosWeg.title: Nicos Weg A1, chapter 8: Appointments (Wann spielen wir?)

points: [[können]] (can) is conjugated in second place, and the other verb goes to the end, unconjugated. In a yes/no question the modal comes first: [[Können Sie mir helfen?]]
Four uses: ability ([[Sie kann gut tanzen.]]), possibility, polite requests ([[Können Sie mir helfen?]]) and permission ([[Du kannst jetzt gehen.]]).
When the meaning is clear, [[können]] can stand alone: [[Ich kann gut Englisch.]] (I speak English well)
Conjugation: [[ich kann]], [[du kannst]], [[er kann]], [[wir können]], [[ihr könnt]], [[sie können]]. The umlaut disappears in the singular.
As with every modal verb, the ich and er/sie/es forms are the same and have no ending.
[[müssen]] (must, have to) works like every modal verb: conjugated in second place (first in a yes/no question), the other verb at the end.
Main use: necessity. [[Ich muss heute lernen.]] (I have an exam.)
It can also give an order, but only from someone in charge, such as parents or a boss: [[Du musst sofort ins Bett!]]
Alone, when it's clear what you mean: [[Ich muss nach Hause.]], [[Ich muss jetzt los.]]
Conjugation: [[ich muss]], [[du musst]], [[er muss]], [[wir müssen]], [[ihr müsst]], [[sie müssen]]. No umlaut in ich, du, er.

phrases.en: Do you have to work tomorrow?
You have to go to bed right now!
You (all) have to listen to me.
He has to work a lot.

points: [[wollen]] (to want) follows the modal pattern: conjugated in second place (first in a yes/no question), the other verb at the end.
Uses: a wish ([[Ich will Pilot werden.]]) and being willing to do something ([[Ich will dir helfen.]]).
Alone, when it's clear: [[Ich will Kaffee.]] It sounds blunt when ordering; [[Ich möchte ...]] is politer.
Conjugation: [[ich will]], [[du willst]], [[er will]], [[wir wollen]], [[ihr wollt]], [[sie wollen]].

phrases.en: I want to become a pilot.
What do you want to do today?
Do you want to come along?

phrases.de: Wir wollen heute Abend ins Kino gehen.
phrases.en: We want to go to the cinema tonight.
He wants to buy some trousers.

points: [[können]] is about what is possible; [[müssen]] about what is necessary: [[Heute kann ich nicht lernen. Ich bin krank.]] versus [[Heute muss ich lernen. Ich habe morgen einen Test.]]

[[können]]: ability ([[Max kann gut singen.]]), possibility ([[Heute kann es schneien.]]), polite requests ([[Können Sie mir helfen?]]), and permission from parents or teachers ([[Du kannst jetzt schreiben.]]).
[[müssen]]: necessity ([[Ich muss morgen arbeiten.]]), orders from parents ([[Du musst sofort ins Bett!]]) and duties in society, at work or in a family ([[Wir müssen einander respektieren.]]).
The situation decides: [[Ich kann morgen arbeiten.]] means you're free to; [[Ich muss morgen arbeiten.]] means you have no choice.
Negated: [[Morgen ist Sonntag, ich muss nicht arbeiten.]] means you don't have to, not that you mustn't.

phrases.de: Tut mir leid, ich kann nicht. Ich muss lernen.
phrases.en: Sorry, I can't. I have to study.

phrases.de: Ohne Brille kann ich nicht lesen.
Mein Auto ist kaputt. Deshalb muss ich heute mit dem Bus fahren.
phrases.en: My car is broken. So I have to take the bus today.

phrases.de: Morgen ist Sonntag, ich muss nicht arbeiten.
phrases.en: Tomorrow is Sunday, I don't have to work.
We have to respect each other.

points: Some prefixes never split off: [[verstehen]] stays in one piece, but [[aufstehen]] splits: [[Ich verstehe.]] but [[Ich stehe auf.]]
You can hear the difference: separable verbs are stressed on the prefix (AUFstehen), inseparable ones on the verb (verSTEHen).
They behave like normal verbs: [[Er versteht mich gut.]], [[Verstehst du mich?]], and with a modal verb they go to the end: [[Ich kann dich verstehen.]]

The prefixes that never split: be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, miss-, ver-, zer-. Examples: [[bekommen]] (to get), [[bezahlen]], [[empfehlen]] (recommend), [[entdecken]] (discover), [[erzählen]] (tell), [[erkennen]] (recognise), [[gehören]], [[gefallen]], [[missverstehen]], [[verkaufen]], [[verlieren]] (lose), [[zerstören]] (destroy).
Watch out: [[bekommen]] means to get or receive, not 'become'.

phrases.de: Wir bekommen bald eine neue Lehrerin.
phrases.en: We're getting a new teacher soon.

phrases.de: Kannst du bitte heute bezahlen? Ich habe kein Geld.
phrases.en: Can you pay today, please? I have no money.

phrases.de: Kannst du mich auf diesem Foto erkennen?
phrases.en: Can you recognise me in this photo?

phrases.de: Wenn ich Schach spiele, verliere ich immer.
phrases.en: When I play chess, I always lose.

notes.extra: Verbs with prefixes that never split ([[verstehen]], [[bezahlen]], [[erzählen]] ...), and how to hear the difference by the stress.

sections.title: You already know this shape
sections.text:
You have used these verbs already: [[Können Sie das bitte wiederholen?]] (Unit 1), and in the song lesson 'Sieben Tage lang': [[Was wollen wir trinken?]] and [[Jetzt müssen wir streiken.]]

All of them have the same shape. The modal verb ([[können]], [[wollen]], [[müssen]]) is in second place, and the main verb goes to the **end**, unchanged (the infinitive):
- [[Ich kann heute nicht kommen.]] = I can't come today.
- [[Ich will Deutsch lernen.]] = I want to learn German.
- [[Ich muss morgen arbeiten.]] = I have to work tomorrow.

The two verbs make a bracket around the rest of the sentence. Germans call it the Satzklammer.

With [[ich]] and with [[er]], [[sie]], [[es]] the form is the same and has no ending: [[ich kann]], [[er kann]] (not 'er kannt'). And the vowel changes in the singular: [[ich muss]] but [[wir müssen]]; [[ich will]] but [[wir wollen]].

sections.title: Separable verbs stay in one piece at the end
sections.text: Without a modal verb, a separable verb splits: [[Ich stehe um sechs auf.]] With a modal verb, it waits at the end in one piece: [[Ich muss um sechs aufstehen.]] [[Kannst du morgen anrufen?]] [[Ich will am Samstag einkaufen.]]

Armenian puts the main verb at the end too: Ես այսօր չեմ կարող գալ is [[Ich kann heute nicht kommen.]], with գալ (to come) last, like [[kommen]]. So the bracket may feel natural.

Russian often keeps the two verbs together (Я не могу прийти сегодня). In a German main clause they split, and everything else goes **between** them.

sections.title: Ich will is not 'I will'
sections.text:
[[Ich will]] means **I want**, like Russian я хочу. It's never the future.

And [[Ich will ...]] can sound pushy when you ask for something in a shop or a café. There, Germans say [[Ich möchte ...]] (I'd like), which comes in Unit 4.

sections.title: muss nicht = don't have to
sections.text:
[[Ich muss nicht arbeiten.]] means I **don't have to** work (there's no need). It does not mean 'I mustn't'. 'Mustn't' is [[darf nicht]], which comes in Unit 5.

- [[Am Sonntag muss ich nicht früh aufstehen.]] = On Sunday I don't have to get up early.

sections.title: Suggesting something: Wollen wir ...?
sections.text:
[[Wollen wir ...?]] = Shall we ...? It's the friendly way to suggest something, as in the song:
- [[Wollen wir zusammen lernen?]] = Shall we study together?
- [[Wollen wir ins Kino gehen?]] = Shall we go to the cinema?

[[ins Kino]] (to the cinema) is a chunk for now. Units 4 and 6 explain the endings of little words like [[ins]].

sections.title: zu Hause, nach Hause
sections.text:
[[zu Hause]] = at home (where you are), [[nach Hause]] = home (where you're going), exactly like Russian дома and домой:
- [[Heute bleibe ich zu Hause.]] = Today I'm staying at home. (дома)
- [[Um sechs gehe ich nach Hause.]] = At six I go home. (домой)

Both are fixed phrases; Unit 6 explains the [[zu]] and the [[nach]].

items.de: Ich kann heute nicht kommen. Ich muss arbeiten.
items.en: I can't come today. I have to work.

items.de: Heute muss ich zu Hause bleiben.
items.en: Today I have to stay at home.

items.note: kommen is left out because it's clear: ... am Sonntag (kommen)

items.en: I still have to do the shopping.

items.de: Was willst du am Wochenende machen?
items.en: What do you want to do at the weekend?
I have to get up at six.

items.instruction: Fill in the gap: I can't come today.
items.explanation: ich kann: no ending with ich. The main verb, kommen, waits at the end.

items.instruction: Fill in the gap: Do you have to work tomorrow? (informal)
items.explanation: du musst. In a yes/no question the modal verb comes first: Musst du morgen arbeiten?

items.prompt: I have to get up early.
items.explanation: muss in second place, aufstehen at the end in one piece.

items.question: Which sentence means 'I want to learn German'?
items.explanation: will in second place, lernen at the end. And remember: ich will = I want, not 'I will'.

items.question: Which sentence means 'I don't have to work today'?
items.explanation: muss nicht = don't have to. kann nicht = can't, will nicht = don't want to.
